title: Byers Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Byers wells have a 240-foot median depth, with typical finished-well costs of $18,000-$28,800.
h1: What Byers Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Well records around Byers show a broad range of conditions across the plains. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median reported depth is 240 feet, while the middle half runs from 100 to 536 feet. Reported yields are generally stronger than many rural areas, but the records are not a guarantee for any individual lot.

Byers sits over the Denver Basin, with permits naming the Arapahoe, unnamed or fractured-bedrock, and Laramie Fox Hills aquifers. Before buying land or pricing a build, check nearby well permits, confirm the permitted use, and have a Colorado well professional review the parcel and access.

sections.heading: Byers well depths vary across the Denver Basin
sections.html:
The median well depth near Byers is 240 feet. The middle half of reported wells falls between 100 and 536 feet, so a bid based only on the median can miss the conditions at a particular lot. The 90th-percentile depth is 680 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 965 feet.

The depth mix shows why location matters: 24% of wells are under 100 feet, 31% are 100-300 feet, 24% are 300-600 feet, and 21% are 600 feet or deeper. Records name the Arapahoe aquifer on 293 wells, an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer on 267, and Laramie Fox Hills on 209. Ask a driller to compare the closest completed wells before accepting a fixed depth assumption.

sections.heading: Water production near Byers is usually adequate, but verify the lot
sections.html:
Among the 388 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0-15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-eight percent report 5-15 gallons per minute, while 32% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No recorded wells in this set fall under 1 gallon per minute or between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

That is encouraging for ordinary household use, but a yield test is still important. Pump yield is not the same as storage in the well, and an individual well can perform differently from its neighbors. Confirm the permitted use before planning livestock, irrigation, or additional residences. Colorado exempt household-use wells also have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: The Byers water level does not show a sharp recorded decline
sections.html:
Only 105 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is smaller than the depth and yield samples. The median depth to water is 80 feet, with the middle half between 60 and 120 feet below the surface.

By decade of measurement, the median was 86 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 80 feet in the 2020s. That series does not indicate a dropping median water table in these records; the later figure is shallower. It is not a guarantee for a new well, because well location, aquifer, pumping, and measurement conditions vary. A driller should review static levels from nearby wells, especially around Byers, Peoria, and Strasburg.

sections.heading: Permit history points to long local drilling experience
sections.html:
The records include 936 permitted wells within the Byers search area, with 524 recorded as constructed. Permitting has continued through the newest permit year, 2025. The largest decade was the 2000s, with 319 permits; the 2010s had 111 and the 2020s had 95.

Crandall Drilling & Pump Service, including records under Crandall Jr. and Howard H., appears most often with 237 wells. Hamacher Well Works Inc. appears on 65, and Paine'S Pump & Repair, including Paine and Burton, appears on 54. These records show who has worked in the area, not a guarantee of availability, price, or current licensing. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: A median-depth Byers well pencils out at a substantial budget
sections.html:
For Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the provided drilling model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 240-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $12,000-$16,800. That figure is only the hole, not a ready-to-use water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $18,000-$28,800 at the median depth. A deeper result can change the total materially, particularly when the well approaches the 536-foot upper edge of the middle half or goes beyond 680 feet. Get the bid in writing and ask what happens if the driller reaches low-producing material, needs extra casing or grout, or must extend electrical and water-line trenches.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic separation, and building limits before closing
sections.html:
Environmental screening matters around Byers. The mapped area within about 10 miles contains 29 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 27 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at a specific parcel, but it is a reason to order a well-water test and review the site history before relying on the well.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even where the area-wide yield statistics look favorable. Have the county and Colorado Division of Water Resources records checked for the exact permit, allowed use, and construction status. Before laying out a house, septic system, drive, or livestock area, confirm setbacks, soil conditions, access for a rig, casing and grout requirements, and the space needed for a replacement well. In an over-appropriated basin, a new use may require an augmentation plan.

sections.heading: Use neighboring Byers wells to price and plan your lot
sections.html:
Start with the closest permitted wells, not an area average. Compare their depths, named aquifers, reported yields, construction records, and static water levels. A lot near Bennett, Brick Center, Comanche Creek, or Deer Trail may provide useful regional context, but nearby wells are more informative than a distant example.

For a purchase, make the contract review include the well permit, recorded construction information, water-quality testing, and a practical yield test. For a build, budget the median finished system as a starting point, then carry room for a deeper hole, electrical work, trenching, and septic construction. Confirm that the intended household, stock, or irrigation use matches the permit. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, resolve water-right and augmentation questions before committing to plans.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Byers, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Byers is 240 feet. The middle half runs from 100 to 536 feet, while 21% of wells are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest recorded well is 965 feet. Nearby completed wells and the aquifer named on the permit are more useful for estimating a specific lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Byers?
faq.a: The drilling model for Byers uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 240-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $12,000-$16,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $18,000-$28,800. A bid can change if the hole must go deeper or requires additional construction work.

faq.q: How much water do Byers wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield near Byers is 11.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-eight percent report 5-15 gallons per minute and 32% report more than 15. These records do not promise the same result on a new lot, so request a yield test.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Byers?
faq.a: Well-water safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. The mapped area within about 10 miles has 29 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 27 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well for relevant contaminants, review site history, and retest after construction or when conditions change.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Byers?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 86 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 80 feet in the 2020s. That comparison does not show a dropping median water table in this dataset. Only 105 wells report static water levels, however, so a buyer should still review measurements from nearby wells and the exact aquifer.
